title: The Fresno Nightcrawler: the most bizarre of all Cryptids
site_name: Dangerous Minds - The weird side of underground culture
excerpt: A look at what makes the study of Cryptids so interesting even if they're not real, via the Fresno nightcrawler and why it became an icon of the region.
content:
Credit: Dangerous Minds / YouTube Still

Tue 27 October 2026 20:45, UK

So, part of the reason that the “study” of cryptids remains such a popular pursuit from Fresno to France is the fact that most of these baffling creatures that fly in the face of everything we know about science are as terrifying as they are strange.

Bigfoot speaks for itself. An eight foot tall beast that can rip you limb from limb, then take you back to its family for mealtime. Beyond the fact that he’s a giant human/moth hybrid, Mothman is an omen of dark times whose appearance means that terrible things will happen to you and yours.

Wendigos? Chupacabras? The Black Shuck? All horrid beasts that will tear your throat out as soon as they look at you, that will be hiding in the one dark corner you fail to look in… should you make the terrible choice of hunting them.

Then there’s the Fresno Nightcrawler. Now, there’s a name that should portent something as dangerous as the others I’ve just mentioned. Honestly, it’s the kind of name that should be attached to some horrifying serial killer or stalker, but no. Instead, it’s the name given to the… Whatever it was captured by cameras belonging to a homeowner named Jose in November 2007. He woke up in the middle of the night to the sound of his dogs barking and ran to check the security cameras of his home in rural Fresno, California.

What he saw was a three foot tall, pale apparition that looked, for all the world, like a pair of ghostly trousers walking jerkily up the dirt road leading up to his house. Another, taller one close behind them.

Jose immediately pressed record and took the resulting footage to Univision, a local Spanish-language television network. The footage was spread around the California paranormal investigation scene and after a second set of the creatures (if you can call them that) were spotted on Yosemite National Park in 2011, the cryptids were fully christened the Fresno Nightcrawler. However, the creature has reportedly popped up much further afoot (lol) than central California.

Sightings of the creatures have been cited everywhere from Montana to as far out of the US as Poland. Now, let’s be real here, this is probably because the Fresno Nightcrawler is a pretty easy visual effect to recreate with a basic understanding of Blender. However, as anyone who’s read The Department of Truth will tell you, the really interesting aspect of cryptids isn’t the idea that they’re actually real, but what part of the human psyche they reflect by believing in them.

Because despite all of the fear and danger surrounding them, people love cryptids. They become symbols of the area they stem from and icons of local tourism. The Fresno Nightcrawler is no different. In fact, there’s something much more understandable about the Nightcrawler becoming plushies, pin badges and mascots because even in the lore, the Nightcrawlers are completely harmless. Right from the off, Jose wasn’t particularly perturbed by seeing them outside his house other than the obvious question of “what the hell is that?!”

Instead, the Nightcrawlers represent the nice side of cryptid culture. They’re bizarre little guys just going about their business, looking a little different from the rest of us. What’s more, they show a different side of Fresno’s culture than most do. The region is known for its agriculture and hardworking lifestyle, but the Nightcrawlers show its soul. It’s not all raisins and harvesting here, there are people who go their own way without hurting anyone. No wonder the cryptid has been embraced by Fresno’s thriving queer scene.

Do they exist? Well, probably not. Though I’m sure you’ll find many people who swear by them if you frequent the right (or possibly very wrong) corners of the internet. However, that’s not the interesting part. The interesting part of the subculture is what these creations say about the ecosystem they were created in. While the Nightcrawler is a little bizarre, it’s harmless, characterful and instantly memorable.

If that can be replicated by a town itself? Then Fresno sounds like a great place to be.
